betterCitation: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, Chapter II, Academy 4:429 (trans. H. J. Paton, 1948)
reason:
NOT REFUTED ON THE WORDS, BUT THE DIVISION IN THE SOURCE LINE IS NOT PATON'S AND SHOULD BE AMENDED.

I attacked this one hardest, because a web search for the sentence in Paton's name came back asserting that Paton's rendering is 'So act as to use humanity, both in your own person and in the person of every other, always at the same time as an end, never simply as a means', which would have made the proposal a different translator's wording under Paton's name and killed it outright. That assertion is wrong, and I proved it wrong rather than argue about it. I downloaded the full OCR of the archive.org scan of The Moral Law (item morallaw029173mbp) and searched every occurrence of 'humanity' in the book. The sentence stands twice, in these two places, and in no other form:

1. In Paton's Analysis of the Argument, under the running heading The Formula of the End in Itself: 'Act in such a way that you always treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never simply as a means, but always at the same time as an end.' This witness carries no footnote markers, so it shows the punctuation clean.

2. In the translation proper: 'The practical imperative will therefore be as follows : Act in such a way that you always treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never simply as a means, but always at the same time as an end. We will now consider whether this can be carried out in practice.' In the scan the words humanity and simply carry superscript footnote references, which the OCR renders as stray marks, and Paton's note at '66, n. 3' is on the word simply, confirming that the markers are notes and not punctuation.

So the proposed wording is Paton's own, letter for letter, including the capital A on Act, which the printed text has because Paton begins the imperative after a colon. Nothing is minted and nothing has drifted.

THE ACADEMY NUMBER IS RIGHT, AND I SAW IT ON THE PAGE. Paton prints the Academy pagination in the margin. In the scan the marginal 429 falls two sentences above, at 'principle of the will and consequently can serve as a practical law', and the marginal 67 of the second German edition falls inside the sentence itself, between 'never simply' and 'as a means'. Academy 4:429 is therefore the right place and is findable in this very edition by its own margins. The date is right too: Hutchinson's University Library published The Moral Law in 1948.

WHAT IS WRONG, AND IT IS SMALL. The source line says 'Second Section'. Paton does not use that division name. His contents page reads Preface 55, Chapter I 61, Chapter II 74, Chapter III 114, and the formula falls inside Chapter II. Second Section is the ordinary scholarly name for Kant's Zweiter Abschnitt and is how Abbott and Gregor head it, but the source line names Paton's translation, and a reader holding Paton will find no Second Section in it. betterCitation replaces it with Chapter II and keeps Academy 4:429, which is printed in Paton's margin and is edition-neutral besides. The amended line is 107 characters, leads with the author's name, carries no dash and no straight quote. I did not refute on this, because the words, the work, the place and the translator are all right and the fix is one phrase; but the line should not ship with a division its own named edition does not print.

EVERY OTHER TEST. shipped.js on the exact wording with 'Immanuel Kant': shipped [], near [], yearCount 2 in months 1 and 7, cap 3, not at cap, not banned. This line therefore closes Kant for the year, which is a deliberate spend and worth saying aloud. No person is doubled in the month: Kant appears once in the verdict directory. Scope is clear: 1785, translation 1948, so not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory, nothing after 1999. There is no speaker to name, since Kant writes in his own voice. Nothing needs a content warning. Tag Philosophy is the form of the work. The quotation ends in a full stop, holds no quotation marks, is prose and is kept as prose. And it is the month's theme in one sentence, stated as a rule for the morning rather than a lament. Ship it with Chapter II.
